channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Day thirteen at Boston Scientific: shipping is largely back, manufacturing is not, and no controller was ever touched
item.description: Boston Scientific is two weeks into recovery from the 25 August intrusion, and the shape of the damage is now settled: an IT-side compromise that stopped a manufacturer anyway. Shipping has been restored for the majority of products at major distribution centres globally, with orders progressively clearing a backlog the company says will take time to work through. Manufacturing is the slower half, and no restoration date has been given. Working with CrowdStrike and other third parties, the company reports growing confidence that access was confined to select internal-facing IT infrastructure, with no malicious activity since 25 August and implanted device function unaffected. No entry route, vulnerability or ransomware claim has been named. For OT defenders the absence is the point: nothing reached a PLC, yet losing the systems that tell a plant what to build and where to ship it has now cost thirteen days. - Boston Scientific incident page and SEC filing, plus SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber recovery reporting — also covered by MedTech Dive, Supply Chain Dive, TechCrunch and CBS News - Detected 25 Aug 2026; disclosed 26 Aug 2026; manufacturing disruption confirmed 28 Aug 2026; company updates 30 Aug 2026 and 4 Sep 2026, the latter confirming majority shipping restoration at major distribution centres, with manufacturing restoration still not declared complete — re-verified 7 Sep 2026, 6:22 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] The water campaign, quantified: CISA counts 100-plus internet-exposed systems hit, with controller logic and alarms altered
item.category: Incident — Confirmed OT disruption, water sector; CISA-quantified scale
item.description: CISA has put a figure on July’s campaign against US water utilities: malicious activity against more than 100 internet-exposed systems in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector, commonly programmable logic controllers wired straight into a cellular modem. The FBI records incidents at utilities in at least seven states since 27 July, with reporting placing targeting across at least a dozen. Some degraded operations — lost pressure, flooding, plants run by hand — though supply was not widely interrupted, and in several intrusions actors altered controllers to disable shutdown processes and alarms, letting unsafe conditions develop unannounced. US officials assess Iranian actors as likely responsible and describe the activity as largely opportunistic. It stays on the page five weeks on because of the admission behind the number: the exposure that carried it was in nobody’s asset register. - CISA exposure-reduction guidance and the FBI/EPA public service announcement — corroborated by SecurityWeek, Cybersecurity Dive, TechCrunch and The Register; Minnesota impact detail from state officials and SecurityWeek - Scale confirmed and reported 26 Aug 2026; observed activity July 2026; FBI PSA issued 30 Jul 2026 — re-verified 7 Sep 2026, 6:22 AM ET

item.title: [High] The water campaign was not the whole campaign — telecoms and energy control systems are now being probed, and there is a $10 million bounty on the man said to run it
item.category: Targeting — Iran-linked campaign widens beyond water into telecommunications and energy; attempts reported, no confirmed OT impact
item.description: Two developments this week moved the summer’s dominant OT story past the water sector. NBC News reported on 2 September, citing four people with access to government and industry threat information, that Iran-linked operators have spent recent weeks probing internet-facing automated control systems at telecommunications and energy providers as well as water utilities — and that those attempts have so far been unsuccessful. A day later the State Department’s Rewards for Justice programme posted a reward of up to $10 million for information identifying or locating Amir Yaryab, named as head of the cyber operations division of the IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command and accused of directing groups including the CyberAv3ngers persona against US critical infrastructure. Separately, a Telegram channel presenting itself as a voice for Iranian cyber operations has threatened action against US energy, water and telecommunications, without evidence of any successful operation. The signal for defenders is the change of aim, not a new capability: the same tradecraft that found exposed water PLCs in July is now being pointed at neighbouring sectors that run the same internet-facing gear. - NBC News reporting on expanded targeting and the State Department Rewards for Justice announcement, as carried by The Record — water-campaign scale from CISA and SecurityWeek - NBC report 2 Sep 2026; $10 million reward announced 3 Sep 2026 — verified 7 Sep 2026, 6:22 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] A small UK generating station ran manually for four days after an Iran-linked cyberattack
item.category: Incident — Confirmed OT disruption, power generation (UK)
item.description: A small British power generating station was taken offline for four days by a cyberattack, with staff forced to restore operations manually. The Telegraph broke the story on 22 August; the UK government confirmed that a small-scale generator had been affected while stating there was at no point a risk to the national energy system, and the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has since contacted power companies about the risk. UK assessments reported by the Telegraph point to hackers affiliated with the Iranian regime, likely the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The site’s size is the uncomfortable part rather than a reassurance: distributed generation, embedded generators and behind-the-meter assets sit below most reporting thresholds, are often remotely operated by a third party, and are numerous enough that an attack that works once is repeatable. - SecurityWeek and CNBC, both citing the originating Telegraph report and the UK government statement - Incident occurred July 2026; reported 22–23 Aug 2026; government response reported 24 Aug 2026 — re-verified 7 Sep 2026, 6:22 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] Five agencies say the S7 family is being actively hunted — and that the exploit scripts are being written with AI
item.category: NSA/CISA/FBI/DOE/EPA joint advisory AA26-231A — active targeting of Siemens S7 series PLCs
item.description: The joint advisory published on 19 August is the primary-source anchor under this edition’s AI research. The NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA report threat actors actively working against Siemens S7 controllers that are internet-exposed or poorly segmented, spanning the S7‑200, ‑300, ‑400, ‑1200 and ‑1500 lines, and name Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Water and Wastewater, Chemical, Food and Agriculture and Commercial Facilities as the most affected sectors. What makes it notable is the method: the agencies describe AI‑generated reconnaissance and exploitation scripts built around the open-source python‑snap7 library and disguised to look like legitimate OT monitoring tooling. Two familiar conditions do the enabling — internet exposure through weak segmentation, and default or weak credentials. The protocol expertise that used to gate ICS exploit development is no longer the barrier. - CISA joint advisory AA26-231A (NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE, EPA) — corroborated by SecurityWeek, Tenable and Infosecurity Magazine - Published 19 Aug 2026 — re-verified 7 Sep 2026, 6:22 AM ET

item.title: [High] A frontier model ported a working PLC exploit to a second controller in eight hours — then bricked it
item.category: Forescout Vedere Labs — AI-assisted exploit development against PLCs
item.description: Forescout’s Vedere Labs published the result of a deliberately awkward experiment: point a frontier AI model at real industrial hardware and see how far it gets. Starting from the team’s own remote code execution exploit for a WAGO 750-852, built on CVE-2021-31886 — a pre-authentication overflow in the Nucleus FTP server — they asked Claude to port it to the related 750-831, giving the model a terminal, Ghidra and the physical device. It worked, but not cleanly. The first model tried failed to trace the vulnerable function; a stronger model eventually worked out why the injected shellcode was being wiped before it could run, and once past that it produced two working payloads in twelve minutes. Total cost of the final stage: over eight hours and more than $500 in API charges. A follow-up attempt at a command-and-control implant wrote to flash and permanently bricked the PLC. - Forescout Research – Vedere Labs report, via SecurityWeek — corroborated by Cybersecurity Dive with direct comment from Vedere Labs - Published 1 Sep 2026; corroborating reporting 1–2 Sep 2026 — verified 7 Sep 2026, 6:22 AM ET

item.title: [High] The router became the implant: a China-nexus crew lived inside Cisco IOS XR and switched off the logs that would have shown it
item.category: Threat intel — China-nexus espionage on carrier-grade routing; critical-infrastructure networks probed
item.description: Sygnia has published an account of an espionage campaign it tracks as Fire Ant operating inside Cisco IOS XR routers — not as a stepping stone to a server, but as the collection platform itself. The actor captured traffic passing through the devices while suppressing the evidence of its own presence, then moved on to the TACACS+ authentication infrastructure and Linux management hosts that sit behind them, harvesting the credentials that administer the rest of the estate. From that position it probed networks associated with critical infrastructure. Sygnia is careful about what it did and did not see: activity against those critical-infrastructure networks was scanning and connection attempts, not established compromise. It assesses strong overlap with operations publicly attributed to the China-nexus cluster UNC3886 without treating the two as the same thing. - Sygnia research, reported by Cybersecurity Dive — also carried by CSO Online, Network World and The Hacker News - Research published and reported early Sep 2026 — re-verified 7 Sep 2026, 6:22 AM ET

item.title: [Medium] Booz Allen benchmarked 18 frontier models and says one can now run an intrusion end to end without a human
item.category: Research — Booz Allen Cyber Weapon Index; 18 frontier models benchmarked for offensive capability
item.description: Booz Allen published The Offensive Frontier: AI as the Attacker on 2 September, drawing on its Cyber Weapon Index — a benchmark run against 18 advanced US and Chinese models. Its headline claim is that at least one frontier model executed a full intrusion chain unaided, from initial access through to network control, marking a shift from AI as an assistant to AI as the operator. The firm’s argument for critical infrastructure is about economics rather than novelty: when the cost, time and expertise needed to run a competent intrusion collapse, capability that was effectively rationed to nation-states becomes available on demand to criminal and non-state actors, and defenders’ response windows narrow accordingly. The report calls for enforceable, sector-specific deadlines requiring operators to demonstrate readiness against AI-enabled attacks. Booz Allen also launched a counter-AI product alongside it, which is worth weighing when reading the urgency. - Booz Allen Hamilton newsroom release and report — reported by Industrial Cyber, Dark Reading and ExecutiveBiz - Report published 2 Sep 2026; reported 4 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] The other remote-access box just went live: public exploit code for a NetScaler auth bypass, and attacks the same week
item.category: Citrix NetScaler ADC/Gateway — CVE-2026-19490, CVSS 9.3, exploitation confirmed
item.description: Citrix patched CVE-2026-19490 on 19 August — an authentication bypass, CVSS 9.3, in NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances configured as a Gateway (SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN or RDP Proxy) or as an AAA virtual server, with SAML configurations among those affected. For a fortnight it stayed theoretical. Then public exploit code appeared in early September, and on 3 September sensor operators began recording bypass attempts from multiple source addresses across four countries, with reporting on 4 September confirming attackers had turned to the flaw in the wild. NetScaler is not an OT product, but it is very often the thing an engineer authenticates through before reaching a jump host, a historian or a vendor session — which makes an unauthenticated bypass on it a route to the plant, not merely to the corporate estate. - Citrix security bulletin, corroborated by BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek and Help Net Security; exploitation telemetry reported by sensor operators - Patched 19 Aug 2026; exploit code public early Sep 2026; exploitation observed 3 Sep 2026; active targeting reported 4 Sep 2026 — verified 7 Sep 2026, 6:22 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] CERT Polska confirms attackers are taking full control of internet-facing MikroTik routers — the box that quietly backhauls half the remote sites in your fleet
item.category: MikroTik RouterOS — “MikroTrick” pre-auth SSH takeover chain, confirmed exploited since 2 Sep
item.description: CERT Polska disclosed six RouterOS vulnerabilities on 5 September and confirmed that two of them are already being chained in live attacks. The chain, named MikroTrick, pairs CVE-2026-67276 (CVSS 9.2) — RouterOS validated only part of an SSH RSA public key, so an attacker who knows a username and the key’s public modulus can forge a key and log in without the private half — with CVE-2026-86060 (CVSS 9.2), a username-parsing flaw that hands the resulting session full administrative rights. Together they give unauthenticated device takeover wherever SSH answers from the internet. A third flaw, CVE-2026-67277 (CVSS 8.8), leaks kernel memory or reboots the device through the unauthenticated bandwidth-test service. MikroTik patched on 3 September in 6.49.21, 7.23.4, 7.24.2 and 7.25beta3. CERT Polska says confirmed compromises trace to 82.192.72.4 and run back to at least 2 September. This matters in OT because RouterOS is the cheap, ubiquitous router behind remote pump stations, substations, wellheads, irrigation skids and contractor-built field cabinets — equipment that is frequently outside the OT asset register and reachable from the internet by design. - CERT Polska (CSIRT NASK) warning and its companion CVE page, with MikroTik’s September 2026 security bulletin — corroborated by The Hacker News and Security Affairs - Patches released 3 Sep 2026; CERT Polska exploitation warning published 5 Sep 2026; attacks observed since at least 2 Sep 2026 — verified 7 Sep 2026, 6:22 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] CISA put SonicWall’s exploited SMA1000 pair in KEV a day after disclosure — a CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw chained to code execution
item.category: SonicWall SMA1000 — Two zero-days exploited, CVSS 10 chain, now in CISA KEV
item.description: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance have been exploited in the wild, and CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 2 September as part of a seven-CVE batch. CVE-2026-83548, carrying a CVSS score of 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface that lets an unauthenticated attacker reach sensitive functionality; CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an OS command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console that an authenticated attacker can turn into remote code execution. SonicWall says it observed exploitation of both, which points to the pair being chained for unauthenticated code execution on the appliance. The vendor found the flaws and the attacks internally, and has published no indicators of compromise. Models 6210, 7210 and 8200v are affected. For OT operators this is the exact class of device that vendor engineers, integrators and on-call staff use to reach the plant from outside — a box that sits at the boundary, terminates trusted sessions and is rarely covered by an OT change window. - SonicWall PSIRT advisory SNWLID-2026-0016 and the CISA KEV addition of 2 Sep 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek and Help Net Security - Advisory published 1 Sep 2026; added to CISA KEV 2 Sep 2026 — verified 7 Sep 2026, 6:22 AM ET

item.title: [High] CISA’s 3 September batch lands on the remote-access client itself — a CVSS 9.6 root-level flaw in IXON VPN
item.category: CISA ICS advisory batch — ICSA-26-246 series; industrial remote access, SCADA platform, engineering tooling
item.description: The five advisories CISA published on 3 September are worth reading in a particular order, because the first one sits on the exact attack path two national agencies spent last week warning about. ICSA-26-246-02 covers CVE-2026-75925 in the IXON VPN Client below 1.4.7, rated CVSS v3.1 9.6: the client’s local configuration interface accepts changes without authenticating the requester, and does not neutralise line-ending sequences before writing them to a file that a privileged subprocess later consumes — so an attacker can inject extra directives and have commands run as root or SYSTEM. The injected configuration survives reboots, and the VPN keeps working normally, so nothing about the machine’s behaviour tells the engineer using it that anything changed. This is the software sitting on maintenance laptops and engineering workstations that reach machines in the field. The rest of the batch is more routine but not trivial: ICSA-26-246-06 flags CVE-2026-77393 in Inductive Automation Ignition 8.1.53 and earlier at CVSS 8.8, where the Gateway’s Create Project Role(s) setting shipped blank and any authenticated user able to run gateway scripts can create projects; ICSA-26-246-03 covers CVE-2026-12663 in Rockwell ControlFLASH 15.07 and earlier, whose installer granted the Everyone group write access to a product directory; ICSA-26-246-01 covers CVE-2026-77477 in the OPC Foundation UA LocalDiscoveryServer installers; and ICSA-26-246-08 covers a missing-authorization issue, CVE-2026-82684, in Tycon Systems TPDIN-Monitor-WEB3 2.2.9 and earlier that could expose credentials, configuration or flash contents. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-246-01, -02, -03, -06 and -08 — summarised by the Viakoo/Security Boulevard daily OT briefing; IXON technical detail cross-checked against the vendor security advisory page and CVE records - Advisories published 3 Sep 2026 — verified 7 Sep 2026, 6:22 AM ET

item.title: [High] CISA’s 1 September batch is five-sixths Rockwell — and it reaches the Logix controllers themselves
item.category: ICSA-26-244-01 to -05 + Rockwell PSIRT — a dozen-plus fixes, controllers included
item.description: CISA published eight ICS advisories on 1 September, and five of them are Rockwell Automation. The set covers RSLinx Classic (ICSA-26-244-01), the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool (-02), the Logix platform (-03), FactoryTalk Activation Manager (-04) and the ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix controller families (-05). The RSLinx item is the one most sites will feel first: four flaws — CVE-2026-9621, CVE-2026-9622, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625 — let crafted Common Industrial Protocol traffic crash the communications service on version 4.50 and earlier, and it stays down until somebody restarts it by hand. RSLinx is the data path between controllers and the HMI, historian and engineering workstations, so a crash there is a visibility outage on a running process, not an IT inconvenience. The batch also carries an update to the Rockwell 1734 POINT I/O advisory (ICSA-26-202-09, Update A) and Update G to the long-running Mitsubishi Electric FA engineering software advisory (ICSA-24-135-04). Rockwell’s own round-up, reported 2 September, puts the total above a dozen fixes and adds detail the CISA summaries do not: remote code execution in FactoryTalk Historian, privilege escalation in FactoryTalk Activation Manager and in the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool, arbitrary code execution through the ControlFLASH firmware utility, cross-site scripting plus a web-server denial of service in ArmorStart distributed motor controllers, and further denial-of-service issues in 1756-ENBT and in Logix controllers via a third-party component. One item needs care rather than alarm: Rockwell’s advisory for CVE-2026-9637, a high-severity denial of service in ControlLogix and CompactLogix, is flagged as exploited in its document header but listed as not exploited in the body, and CISA states it is not aware of exploitation — read it as a documentation inconsistency, not a live campaign, and patch it on its merits. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-244-01 through -05 published 1 Sep 2026, plus ICSA-26-202-09 Update A and ICSA-24-135-04 Update G, read against the Rockwell Automation security advisory index and SecurityWeek’s 2 Sep 2026 round-up of the full Rockwell set - Published 1 Sep 2026 — verified 7 Sep 2026, 6:22 AM ET

item.title: [Medium] The monitoring requirement just followed the adversary out of the electronic security perimeter
item.category: NERC CIP-015-2 — Internal network monitoring extends past the ESP
item.description: NERC’s FERC-directed deadline to modify CIP-015-1 fell on 2 September 2026. The change is small to read and large to implement: internal network security monitoring, until now required only inside the electronic security perimeter, is extended to electronic access control or monitoring systems and physical access control systems that sit outside it. FERC’s reasoning is the one every responder recognises — you cannot claim visibility inside a perimeter while the systems that grant access to it are unwatched. Compliance is phased: 2 September 2028 for high-impact BES cyber systems and for medium-impact systems with external routable connectivity in control centres and backup control centres, and 2 September 2030 for the remaining applicable medium-impact systems. Two years is less than it sounds when the sensors need budget cycles. - NERC petition to FERC for approval of CIP-015-2, with analysis from Dragos, Nozomi Networks and Industrial Cyber - FERC-directed modification deadline 2 Sep 2026; compliance dates 2 Sep 2028 and 2 Sep 2030 (forward-looking) — verified 7 Sep 2026, 6:22 AM ET

item.title: [Medium] The free assessment most small utilities actually used is being withdrawn — and nothing at that price replaces it
item.category: Policy — CISA ends six free critical-infrastructure assessments; direct impact on small utilities and municipal operators
item.description: CISA is stopping six of the free cybersecurity assessments it has offered critical-infrastructure operators, according to reporting on an internal 25 August meeting in which the acting head of the agency’s Integrated Operations Division told staff to cease performing them. All six were regional-adviser engagements — an adviser sits with an operator, works through structured questions using the agency’s Cyber Security Evaluation Tool, and produces a report of prioritised improvements — and they covered intrusion detection and containment, ransomware readiness and supply-chain risk. The change follows the loss of roughly a third of CISA’s workforce. The operators affected are the ones with the least capacity to absorb it: small water systems, rural electric co-ops, municipal transit and county government, for whom a free structured assessment was often the only external review they would ever get. Commercial equivalents exist; they are not priced for a utility serving four thousand people. - Cybersecurity Dive reporting, carried by Utility Dive — based on an internal CISA meeting; no formal agency notice published as of this edition - Direction given 25 Aug 2026; reported 3 Sep 2026 — verified 7 Sep 2026, 6:22 AM ET

item.title: [Medium] Britain moves to take the power to disconnect your suppliers — and a four-day generator outage is what tabled the amendment
item.category: UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill — Supplier designation powers, UK
item.description: Late amendments to the UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill would give ministers power to stop critical-sector organisations using technology suppliers judged high risk. The Bill was introduced in November 2025, has cleared the Commons and sits in the Lords as HL Bill 32, close to Royal Assent; the amendments were tabled on 24 August, two days after reporting that Iran-linked actors had forced a small UK generating site offline for four days (see Incidents & Attacks). The approach is a departure worth noting: rather than only demanding better in-house security from operators, it lets government cut them off from third parties it considers inadequately secured, regardless of the supplier’s size or sector. The Bill already carries strict incident-reporting timelines and heavy penalties. Practitioners quoted in the coverage make the obvious point — a small integrator or managed service provider with standing remote access into a plant may not think of itself as critical national infrastructure, but a designation regime will decide that for it. - SecurityWeek reporting on the tabled amendments, read against the UK government’s Cyber Security and Resilience Bill collection on gov.uk - Amendments tabled 24 Aug 2026; reported 2 Sep 2026; Bill awaiting Royal Assent — verified 7 Sep 2026, 6:22 AM ET

item.title: [Medium] On Friday, anyone selling a connected product into the EU owes a 24-hour warning on exploited vulnerabilities
item.category: EU Cyber Resilience Act — Reporting obligations effective 11 Sep 2026
item.description: The EU Cyber Resilience Act enters its reporting phase this Friday, 11 September 2026 — four days from this edition. From that date, manufacturers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents affecting their products, with an early warning inside 24 hours and a fuller notification inside 72 hours. The scope reaches far past consumer IoT: PLCs, RTUs, drives, gateways, HMIs, protocol converters and the engineering software around them are products with digital elements, and the obligation follows the manufacturer regardless of where the affected device is installed. Legal analysts advise naming an owner now and building the assessment, escalation and customer-communication path in advance, coordinating it with existing NIS2 and GDPR duties rather than standing up a third parallel process. - Freshfields analysis via Lexology, surfaced in the Viakoo/Security Boulevard daily OT briefing - Analysis published 1 Sep 2026; obligations effective 11 Sep 2026 (forward-looking) — verified 7 Sep 2026, 6:22 AM ET

item.title: [Medium] TSA quietly reshapes what rail and transit must report — and shrinks the covered population from 846 operators to 67
item.category: TSA — Surface transportation cyber collection revised; comments close 1 Oct 2026
item.description: TSA sent OMB a revised information collection for cybersecurity measures across freight rail, mass transit and passenger rail, and over-the-road bus, published in the Federal Register on 1 September with comments due 1 October. The substance of the security directives is unchanged: designate a primary and alternate Cybersecurity Coordinator, report cyber incidents to CISA within 72 hours, maintain a Cybersecurity Incident Response Plan, and complete assessments against the TSA form. What has changed is the accounting and the maintenance burden. The estimate falls to 67 respondents and 22,167 annual hours, from 846 respondents and 210,684 hours, because most covered operators have already satisfied the one-time submissions; the revision instead formalises the recurring obligations — keeping response plans current, filing annual Cybersecurity Assessment Plan reports, updating Implementation Plans — plus a January 2026 rule that any non-US-citizen Cybersecurity Coordinator hold NEXUS, Global Entry or an equivalent vetted-traveller status. - Federal Register notice 2026-17894 (TSA / OMB review) — reported by Industrial Cyber - Published 1 Sep 2026; reported 2 Sep 2026; comment period closes 1 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] Six national cyber agencies just published the part of incident response that operators keep improvising: what you tell people while the plant is down
item.category: Six-nation joint guidance — communicating during IT and OT service outages
item.description: CISA and the FBI, with Canada’s CCCS, the UK NCSC, Australia’s ACSC and New Zealand’s NCSC, released joint guidance on 2 September covering communications during IT and operational-technology outages. The recommendations are unglamorous and, judging by this year’s incidents, badly needed: define notification thresholds and audiences before an event, write in plain language rather than legal hedging, say explicitly what is known, what is not, and what is still being investigated, then update on a stated cadence instead of when there is good news. It also asks that outage messaging be aligned with operational security, law-enforcement engagement and containment work, so that a status page does not disclose what responders are still trying to keep quiet. For OT operators the framing matters: this treats a control-system outage as a public-facing event with customers, regulators, downstream operators and staff who all need different messages on different clocks. - CISA / FBI joint guidance with CCCS, NCSC-UK, ACSC and NCSC-NZ — corroborated by Industrial Cyber and The Cyber Express - Published 2 Sep 2026
